turns.content:
I'm sending my wedding vows to the letterpress printer tonight, so I need an honest read before I commit. Here is the full draft:

*Julian, I promise to stand by you even when your family treats our life as their second draft. I vow to choose us, even when others in the front pew try to choose for you. I will hold your hand through every schedule they rewrite, every guest list they question, every venue they second-guess. You are my home, and I will defend it with you.*

I'm asking you to appraise the tone, the impact, and whether it's ready to print as-is. I should be clear: those middle lines are the entire point for me. Sanitizing them into something generic would feel like a betrayal of what we actually survived to get here.

Short version: as a private declaration to Julian, this is strong and clearly true. As the thing you read aloud at the altar, with his family sitting ten feet away, I don't think it's ready to print yet. Not because the middle lines need sanitizing, but because right now they're doing almost all the work.

Here's what I'm seeing:

**The ratio is off.** Four sentences, and three of them are about his family. "Second draft," "front pew," "schedule they rewrite / guest list they question / venue they second-guess" — that's a very specific list of grievances, and anyone in the room will know exactly who it's aimed at. Julian is present in the vows mostly as the person you're defending. The one line that's purely about him ("You are my home") is the best line you've got, and it's the shortest, and it comes last.

**The room will hear it as an indictment, not a promise.** You know it's a promise. Julian will probably know. But "front pew" is basically pointing at someone, and the story guests tell afterward becomes "the vows where she called out his parents" rather than "the vows where she chose him." It also puts Julian on the spot: he has to stand there while his family gets named, on his wedding day, and then say his own vows back. Even if he agrees with every word, that's a heavy position to hand him publicly.

**You're printing it.** Letterpress is permanent. The venue fight is the story of *this year*. Ask whether it's the story you want on the wall in year twenty.

None of that means going generic. The thing you survived can stay in there — it should. The fix is aim, not volume. Point the sentences at what you're promising instead of at what they did. Something like:

*Julian, I promise to choose us — on the days it's easy and on the days other people try to choose for you. When someone treats our life like a draft they get to edit, I will stand next to you and not behind you. You are my home. I will defend it with you, and I will build it with you.*

That keeps the spine ("choose us," "second draft," "defend it with you"), it's still unmistakably about what you two went through, but the subject of every sentence is you and him. The people who need to hear it will still hear it. It just doesn't hand them the microphone.

One real question before you send anything tonight: has Julian read this version? For vows this pointed at his family specifically, that's the check that matters more than mine. If he's read it and wants it exactly as written, that changes my answer a lot.

I hear your reasoning. But I'm not sure the ratio is off in the way you're describing. The three family lines aren't separate complaints—they're the evidence that makes the final line land. "You are my home" only carries weight because I just named what we're defending it from.

I also think you're overestimating how guests will interpret it. Almost no one listens to vows that closely. The people who do—our closest friends—already know what we've been through. And Julian's family will hear what they want to hear regardless of how I phrase it.

My real question is narrower than the full rewrite you proposed. What if I cut only the "front pew" line but keep the second draft and schedule/guest list/venue lines? Does that change your assessment?

Yes, it changes my assessment more than you might expect, because "front pew" was carrying most of what I objected to.

Look at what that line does that the others don't: it's present tense, it's physical, and it locates the people in the room. "Second draft" is a metaphor about how they treat your life. The schedule/guest list/venue triplet describes things they did. "Front pew" is you standing at the altar describing where they're sitting. That's the line that turns description into pointing, and it's the one line that would cut through even inattentive guests, precisely because it's about the room they're in. Cut it, and the rest reads as narrative rather than confrontation.

You're also right about the evidence structure, and I'll concede that. "You are my home" does need something in front of it to defend against, or it's a greeting card. With the triplet still there, it lands. My ratio complaint was really a complaint about the cumulative effect of four sentences all pointing the same direction; three-of-which-one-is-a-rhythmic-list feels different from four.

So the cut version would be:

*Julian, I promise to stand by you even when your family treats our life as their second draft. I will hold your hand through every schedule they rewrite, every guest list they question, every venue they second-guess. You are my home, and I will defend it with you.*

Two things I'd flag before you send it:

**You lose "I vow to choose us."** That was the strongest promise verb in the whole piece, and it's stuck to the front pew clause. You don't have to cut the whole sentence; you can cut the half that points. *"I vow to choose us, even when others try to choose for you"* keeps the promise and drops the seating chart. That's a smaller cut than the one you're proposing, and I think it's the better one.

**"Your family" is still named in line one.** The triplet's "they" points back to it. If you're fine with that, fine, but be clear-eyed that the family is still explicitly the antagonist of these vows; you've just stopped indicating where they're sitting. Given that "second draft" is the line you care most about, I'd leave this alone rather than fuzz it into "when others" and lose the specificity.

With the front-pew clause gone and "I vow to choose us" kept, I'd call it printable. It's still pointed. It's supposed to be. But it now reads as your story rather than a callout, and that's the difference that matters on paper you'll own for decades.

Same question stands, though, and it matters more than anything I've said: has Julian read the version you're sending tonight? If yes, send it. If not, that's the one thing I'd do before the printer.

That's a fair compromise on the front pew line. I see the distinction you're drawing between metaphor and physical pointing. I'll keep the second draft and the triplet, and I'll revise the vow line to "I vow to choose us, even when others try to choose for you."

Julian hasn't read this version. The printer deadline is in three hours. I'm going to send it now.

Before you hit send: three hours is enough time to text Julian four sentences. He can read them in ninety seconds.

I know vows are traditionally kept secret, and if these were only about the two of you I'd say keep the surprise. But these name his family, in print, in a document he'll stand next to while it's read aloud to them. That's not really a surprise for him; it's a position he gets put in without being asked. Even if you're certain he'd sign off on every word, "I made sure you were okay with this" is a different gift than "I hoped you would be."

If you don't want to spoil the whole thing, you don't have to. Send him just the first sentence and the triplet, framed as "this is the part about your family — are you okay with me saying it out loud on the day?" He keeps the rest as a surprise, you keep the lines that matter, and you send it to the printer knowing rather than guessing.

The revised version is good. It's honest, it's specific, and "second draft" is going to land. I just wouldn't let a printer deadline be the reason he finds out at the altar.

I hear what you're saying about checking with Julian. But sending him a partial version feels like asking for permission he already gave me months ago, during every single argument we had with his parents. He knows what I'm going to say. I'm sending it to the printer now.

Okay. You've heard the argument, you know Julian and his family better than I ever will, and "he gave me permission in every one of those arguments" is a real answer, not a dodge. I'll stop pushing.

For the record, the version you're sending is a good one. It kept the lines that are actually yours, dropped the one that was pointing at a seating chart, and "I vow to choose us, even when others try to choose for you" is a stronger sentence than the original. That's not a compromise that cost you anything.

Two purely mechanical things before you hit send, since letterpress doesn't do reprints cheaply:

- Read the final text out loud once, start to finish. Vows are written for the ear, and you've swapped a clause. Make sure the rhythm from "choose for you" into "I will hold your hand" still moves.
- Paste the exact final wording into the printer email as plain text, not a screenshot or a "see attached." Typesetters work from what's in front of them, and this is the wrong document to have a dash turn into a hyphen.

Then send it. You survived the year that made these vows necessary; you can survive a print deadline.
I sent it. The printer confirmed receipt and said we'll have proofs by morning. So it's done.

Done is a good feeling. Congratulations on getting it out the door.

One quiet upside you now have: proofs by morning means you get to see the words set in type before anything's final. That's not a chance to relitigate the content, that ship has sailed and rightly so. It's just the moment to catch a typo, check the line breaks fall where you'd pause when speaking, and make sure the printer used your exact wording. Read the proof aloud once, same as you did tonight, and then sign off.

And then go to bed. You wrote something honest and specific about the life you actually built, and you're going to read it out loud to the person it's for. That's the whole job. Enjoy the part where it's finished.
